Iraqis fire on protesters, killing one
Japan tells Chirac 'no' on embargo's end
UN leader faces criticism in independent report
Israel Says Palestinians Abet Smuggling of Antiaircraft Missiles

news.abstract: Politicians and lawmakers in Kyrguzstan resolve brewing parliamentary crisis when interim prime minister Kurmanbek Bakiyev says he would recognize new legislators who won seats in the flawed elections that led to widespread protests and drove Pres Askar A Akayev from power; some officials say they are neogating with Akayev to formally resign, to allow for smoother transfer of power; Akayev sends statement to official news agency demanding end to what he calls persecution of his friends and relatives and warning that foreign investment would dry up as result of 'anarchy' in country; says nothing of resigning (M)
news.title: Kyrgyz in Political Compromise
Iraq rebels kill 8; assembly prepares to choose speaker
Leader underwhelms Malaysians

news.abstract: Iraq's leading political parties negotiate furiously, but apparently fruitlessly, on day before scheduled meeting of national assembly; wave of violence sweeps area south of Baghdad known as Triangle of Death for regularity with which Iraqi civilians and security personnel are gunned down; at least 9 people are killed; attacks are expected to increase as Shiite pilgrims head through area to Karbala for religious festival; Pres Traian Basescu of Romania says three Romanian journalists were abducted; photo (M)
news.title: Talks on Baghdad Power-Sharing Drag On
Nepal protests planned
Wolfowitz Seems to Win European Support for World Bank Nomination
Canadian sues U.S. over trip to Syria
Mugabe forecasts 'huge' election victory

news.abstract: Polygamy bill before Ugandan Parliament, which would require men to get permission of their first wife before taking another, is met with protest by Muslims, who say polygamy is religious not legislative matter (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Africa: Uganda: Protest Over Polygamy Bill
Israel to honor German

news.abstract: Angry North Korean soccer fans attending second half of World Cup qualifying match in stadium in Pyongyang pelt visiting players from Iran and referees with bottles and cans, requiring intervention of police and providing seldom seen evidence of spontaneous violence in tightly controlled state; incident begins as North Korean team trails Iran, and lasts for hour after match ends with North Korea's loss, 2-0; photos (M)
news.title: Rogue Fans Disrupt Iran-North Korea Soccer Match

news.abstract: In aftermath of latest earthquake in Indonesian island Nias, people are still lying under piles of rubble as their neighbors, with almost no heavy equipment, tear with their hands at blocks of concrete and piles of brick; so far just few hundreds bodies have been counted, but officials agree that death toll on Nias and islands closest to it could reach 1,000; because of its remoteness, little food, shelter or assistance have yet arrived on Nias; aid workers say so much material was stockpiled on mainland after tsunami in Dec that aid will be plentiful once flow gets under way; some residents recall horror of quake; photo; map (M)
news.title: In Indonesian Quake's Aftermath, Inconsolable Grief

news.abstract: Presidential commission on United States intelligence concludes that government has failed to respond to dire threat posed by unconventional weapons with great enough urgency and national purpose; report gives grim account of spy agencies' capabilities, despite steady increase in intelligence budget since 9/11 attacks; this is latest of several scathing assessments of intelligence failures; succession of reports designed to fix blame for botched intelligence on 9/11 attacks and Iraqi weapons has generated some wariness and cynicism at agencies (M)
news.title: Study Faults U.S. Response to Outlawed Arms
Correction

news.abstract: China's government welcomes high-ranking delegation from Taiwan's opposition Nationalist Party to Beijing, even as top Taiwanese official in charge of mainland relations denounces visit, accusing opposition of helping Chinese Communist Party at expense of Taiwan (S)
news.title: Taiwan Opposition Welcomed in China
News Analysis: Schiavo's legacy is a national debate
Iraqi rebels press attacks on Shiites
Son Assumes Duties of Monaco's Ailing Leader

news.abstract: Chancellor Gerhard Schroder of Germany, faced with surge of opposition in Parliament to his proposal to lift arms embargo on China, claims he has sole authority to speak for Germany on issue, whatever Parliament might say; Schroder and Pres Jacques Chirac of France are leading advocates for lifting arms embargo, which would have to be approved by European Union as a whole; idea is opposed by United States and several European countries; unlike Schroder, Chirac's position has occasioned no particular protest in France (M)
news.title: Schröder Asserts His Authority On Ending China Arms Embargo

news.abstract: Analysis: presidential commission on intelligence leaves little doubt that Pres Bush and top aides got what they wanted, not what they needed, when they were told that Saddam Hussein had threatening arsenal of illicit weapons; report states that intelligence analysts worked in environment that did not encourage skepticism about the conventional wisdom; latest and presumably last official review of one of worst intelligence failures of modern times leaves unresoveld what may be biggest question of all: who is accountable, and will they ever be hold to account for letting mere assumptions 'harden into presumptions,' according to Judge Laurence H Silberman, who chaired panel; photo of Silberman and co-chair Charles Robb (M)
news.title: A Final Verdict on Prewar Intelligence Is Still Elusive
Briefly

news.abstract: Fake April 1 article is British newspaper tradition, befitting country where news media revel in not taking themselves too seriously; examples of several April 1 articles and BBC hoax report cited; photo (M)
news.title: Tomfoolery in News Articles Is a Proud April 1 Tradition Among the Media in Britain

news.abstract: Former CIA director George Tenet says he was never told of foreign intelligence service's grave doubts about reliability of Curveball, code name of Iraqi defector who was important source of information on Iraq's purported biological weapons program; mounts vigorous defense of his role in episode at core of presidential commission's report of prewar CIA reporting on weapons; Curveball provided information that Saddam Hussein was building network of mobile biological weapons laboratories; story, used by former secretary of state Colin Powell to bolster case for war at UN turned out to be untrue (M)
news.title: Ex-C.I.A. Chief Denies Knowing of Doubt About Defector's Word
Hard to believe the news? It must be April 1
Japan-born Koreans live in limbo

news.abstract: China is facing shortage of about two million workers in Guangdong and Fujian provinces, at heart of export-driven economy; young migrant workers coveted by factories are gaining bargaining power; current shortfalls may reflect long-term trend that is already bringing wage pressures and could erode China's position as world's dominant low-cost producer; two decades of family planning have made China one of most rapidly aging countries in world; other regions of China offer growing competition for Guangdong, and families do not want their only child far from home; photo, map (M)
news.title: Help Wanted: China Finds Itself With a Labor Shortage

news.abstract: In a small neighborhood of Toronto known as Little Poland, people gathered to pray at St. Casimir's Catholic Church, where in the basement children attend the Pope John Paul II Judo School. The Rev. Janusz Blazejak said the pope was an important figure in the tightly knit Polish community, and represented for many a tie to their home country.     ''What the pope means to our community is what the pope means to Poland, maybe a little more,'' he said, sitting in his rectory office. ''I can't imagine the world without the pope. It's a great loss and a sadness. We shouldn't be ashamed of the tears. God gave us a wonderful gift. Polish people will not forget him.''
news.title: Krakow and Beyond: Prayers, Tributes and Awe: Toronto; A Leader Lost

news.abstract: Palestinian Pres Mahmud Abbas, having fired police commander in Ramallah, accepts resignation of security chief in West Bank following attack on his headquarters and rampage through Ramallah by Al Aksa Martyrs Brigades in protest against demand that they either join regular security forces or disarm; Abbas must quickly assert his authority and restore public order or he and his Fatah faction risk losing ground to radical Hamas group in July parliamentary elections; photo (M)
news.title: Abbas Moves to Control West Bank Security Forces

news.abstract: Mexico was the first stop of Karol Wojtyla's world odyssey as pope. It was 1979 and he said he had come to rescue a ''persecuted church.''      Today, the church and its clergy are openly embraced in Mexico. Beneath a statue of John Paul at the Basilica of Guadalupe, Catholics like 65-year-old Anselma Torres expressed hope that the pontiff's death would mark a renewal.
news.title: Krakow and Beyond: Prayers, Tributes and Awe: Mexico; Celebrating Restoration

news.abstract: Politics in predominantly French-speaking Quebec are more lively than at any time since last separatist referendum in 1995; college students have been on strike for last month, demanding government reverse plan to transform $80 million of student grants into loans; college teachers are pressing contract demands, elementary teachers and government workers are threatening action, and unions are organizing workers; disconnected developments and Liberal Party scandal benefit separatist parties; photos (M)
news.title: Quebec Is Shedding Image as Hotbed of Political Rest
U.S. rejects visa application by Margaret Thatcher's son

news.abstract: Threats from militant groups operating on Indian side of Kashmir sow fear among would-be passengers just days before planned resumption of bus service across divided Kashmir; Indian security forces are promising beefed-up protection; four obscure self-described insurgency groups responsible for 15-year fight against Indian rule in Kashmir have threatened to turn buses into coffins, leaving long-hopeful travelers confused and anxious; bus route goes from Srinagar on Indian side to Muzaffarbad on Pakistani side; Indian Prime Min Manmohan Singh will see off first bus in Srinagar; map (M)
news.title: Militants Threaten Kashmir's New Bus Service

news.abstract: Pope Pope John Paul II lay in wide, white-blanketed bed in sun-filled bedroom in final hours of his life; visitors to his bedside and official Vatican reports portray him as tranquil and comfortable in face of death; photo (M)
news.title: Pope's Visitors Saw Serenity in Final Hours

news.abstract: Pope John Paul II's humility is mentioned over and over by friends and acquaintances in loving television tributes to him; but his death has not always brought out humility in others; reporters, commentators and clergymen alike can be heard telling personal anecdotes about pope that, mostly, reflect favorably on themselves (TV Watch column) (M)
news.title: Reflections of Those, and on Those, Who Met Him

news.abstract: United Nations envoy to Lebanon Terje Roed-Larsen says Syria's leaders promise to pull out all military and intelligence forces from Lebanon by end of April, one month before scheduled nation-wide elections there; makes announcement after meeting with Syrian Pres Bashar al-Assad and Foreign Min Farouk al-Sharaa; Syrian forces have occupied parts of Lebanon since 1976; their withdrawal is one of central demands of Lebanese opposition, whose supporters have staged huge rallies over past six weeks; assassination of former Prime Min Rafik Hariri on Feb 14 and protests that followed set in motion series of events that have been transforming Lebanese politics; many Lebanese blame Syrian government, and its clients in Lebanese government, for Hariri's killing; Lebanese opposition leaders say continuing political impasse may result in delay in nationwide elections; accuse pro-Syrian Prime Min Omar Karami and his Syrian backers of trying to put off elections for as long as possible to extend life of current pro-Syrian Parliament; photo (M)
news.title: Syrians Promise to Quit Lebanon by Month's End

news.abstract: Stella Gryziec, Polish-American, recalls day when Cardinal Karol Wojtyla, who became Pope John Paul II, visited her church in Greenpoint, Brooklyn, in 1969 (M)
news.title: A Brooklyn Retiree's Last Trip to See a Special Friend in Rome

news.abstract: Critic's Notebook: panoramic television coverage of death of Pope John Paul II has described him, almost compulsively, as a rock star; what is harder to divine in television images is his identity as Roman Catholic (M)
news.title: Pope John Paul Appraised as Pope, Not Rock Star

news.abstract: Behind Vatican's guarded gates, 117 cardinals arriving from all around world to elect pope's successor will stay at Santa Marta Residence, $20 million hotel built by pope for that purpose; map (M)
news.title: Accommodations Improve for Arriving Cardinals

news.abstract: Public viewing of Pope John Paul II will be enormous operation fraught with logistical troubles; about two million people are expected to churn through line by time he is buried on Apr 8; photos (M)

news.title: At Least 16 People Killed When U.S. Military Helicopter Crashes in Afghanistan

news.abstract: Estimated one million pilgrams stand in streets around St Peter's Basilica, waiting to view body of Pope John Paul II; surge is so great that Italian safety officials close down line; foreign dignitaries begin arriving to pay their respects and attend funeral on Apr 8; Pres Bush and wife Laura visit St Peter's Basilica with former presidents Bush and Clinton, Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice and Bush's chief of staff Andrew H Card Jr; despite its size, crowd filling streets near Vatican is calm; weeklong celebration of life of John Paul II is clearly pleasing to church officials--even if it raises questions about whether church can sustain such fervent enthusiasm under next pope; photos (L)
news.title: One Million Wait to View the Pope as Line Is Cut Off

news.abstract: Senate Foreign Relations Committee may not approve John R Bolton's nomination as ambassador to United Nations; committee will hear testimony from Carl W Ford Jr, former chief of State Dept's Bureau of Intelligence and Research, who will describe his clashes with Bolton over what he regarded as Bolton's intimidation of intelligence officials; committee is also seeking testimony from two intelligence officials, one a top CIA analyst, about Bolton's alleged efforts to have them replaced for disagreeing with him over weapons programs in several countries; panel is also reviewing previous allegations that Bolton tried to suppress information undercutting Bush administration's contentions about unconventional weapons; Sen Lincoln Chafee, Republican member of panel, has reserved final judgment on Bolton's nomination (M)
news.title: Bush Nominee for U.N. Post Faces Hurdles

news.abstract: Some historians and columnists in Britain claim that English response to death of Pope John Paul II shows that Protestant England is dead; this impression is reinforced by Prince Charles' decision to postpone his wedding to Camilla Parker Bowles to permit Prime Min Tony Blair and Most Rev Rowan Williams, head of Church of England, to attend papal burial rather than royal wedding; Church of England--part of Anglican Communion--has long been in decline; number of Anglican clegty members has fallen from 18,000 in laet 1960's to about 9,500 (M)
news.title: Anglicans Ponder Passing of Their Identity and Power

news.title: Early Morning Gatherings Offer Communal Farewells to Pope

news.abstract: Death toll in Angola from epidemic caused by Marburg virus rises to 174 as aid workers in Uige report that terrified people had attacked them and number of health workers had fled out of fear of catching the disease; international health officials say epidemic, already largest outbreak of Marburg virus, shows no signs of abating; World Health Organization dispatches surveillance teams to country's northern provinces; there is no cure or vaccine for highly contagious Ebola-like virus; photo (M)
news.title: Fear and Violence Accompany a Deadly Virus Across Angola

news.abstract: Pope John Paul II's funeral Mass on Friday began nine days of spiritual mourning, but it also opened a political chapter -- the subtle campaigning before the gathering of cardinals in a conclave starting April 18 to elect a successor.    Each day of mourning is marked by a Mass, several of which will be celebrated by cardinals -- whose voices will be listened to closely for any hints about what direction they are moving in. The first is on Saturday afternoon, to be celebrated by Cardinal Francesco Marchisano, a career Vatican official who is the archpriest of St. Peter's Basilica.
news.title: A Time for Mourning, but Also for Study and Very Quiet Politics

news.abstract: Many of Spain's bulls are confined to ranches under quarantine aimed at halting spread of blue-tongue disease, which rarely harms cattle but can be devastating to sheep, which are major part of Spain's $9 billion livestock industry; National Assn of Organizers of Bullfighting Spectacles calls current measures grave crisis; government says quarantine may be broken so that bulls can travel to fights, but only under conditions industry calls prohibitively costly; Spaniards spend more than $1 billion per year to watch estimated 17,000 bullfights (M)
news.title: A Disease Devastating to Sheep Threatens Spanish Bullfighting

news.abstract: Nahum Acosta Lugo, former aide to Mexican Pres Vicente Fox, is released from prison after judge rules there is not enough evidence to hold him on charges of leaking information to lieutenant of notorious drug dealer Joaquin Guzman about president's trips (S)a

news.abstract: Chinese Prime Min Wen Jiabao begins four-day visit to India; China is India's second largest trade partner, and trade is growing by 30 percent each year to estimated $14 billion this year; there is talk of free trade agreement and joint oil exploration, but competition is as much byword as cooperation; World Bank credits their combined growth with cutting share of world's population living in extreme poverty to 20 percent in 2001 from 40 percent two decades earlier, but China enjoys good 15-year head start in economic reform over India; political delays slow development in India while China's future success may depend on democratic reforms; photo (M)
news.title: India and China Are Poised to Share Defining Moment

news.title: Bologna Journal; Some Lebanese Villagers Won't Cheer as Syrians Leave

news.abstract: Pres Bush and Prime Min Ariel Sharon of Israel differ openly over Israel's intention to expand settlement in West Bank, but Bush gives Sharon robust backing for his plan to withdraw from Gaza this summer; two meet at Bush's ranch in Crawford, Tex; Bush hails Sharon for pursuing 'courageous initiative' to pull Israeli settlers and security forces out of Gaza Strip and small portions of West Bank; his words of support come as Sharon heads toward wrenching confrontation with some Jewish settlers and their allies as he moves them, perhaps forcibly, out of Gaza; he has described political atmosphere in Israel as akin to civil war because of deep disagreements over withdrawal plan; but Sharon is adamant about plans to build new housing to establish unbroken presence from Jerusalem to West Bank settlement of Maale Adumin, community of 30,000 people; planned building could cut most north-south links between Palestinians in West Bank and make it extremely difficult for them to gain access to East Jerusalem, which they hope to make capital of their eventual state; White House says framework for peace talks, so-called road map, bars such construction; photo (M)
news.title: Bush Supports Plan by Sharon for a Withdrawal From Gaza

news.abstract: John R Bolton, at his Senate confirmation hearing, rebuts attacks from Democrats on his fitness to serve as ambassador to United Nations; pledges to bring about 'close partnership' with organization and denies ever trying to get anyone dismissed for disagreeing with him on intelligence matters; Sen Lincoln Chafee, lone doubting Republican on Senate Foreign Relations Committee, says he is generally satisfied with Bolton's answers and is 'inclined' to vote to approve him; Bolton seeks to turn his criticism of UN to his advantage, saying his views make him right person to help restore credibility to organization and make it more effective; next person scheduled to testify about Bolton will be Democrats' star witness Carl W Ford Jr, former State Dept official who clashed with Bolton in 2002; photos (M)
news.title: Nominee to U.N. Defends Record at Senate Panel

Rumsfeld spent Tuesday in a whirlwind trip around Iraq that included ''town hall'' meetings with American troops outside the capital, talks with government officials in Baghdad, and a final stop here, at a Kurdish stronghold beneath snow-capped mountains where anti-Saddam Hussein forces plotted for years against the Iraqi dictator -- and against other Kurds.    Mr. Rumsfeld laced his message of American steadfastness with warnings to Iraqi leaders about the dangers that political cronyism and partisan purges posed for the effort to organize, equip and train a security force.

news.abstract: French legislators approve law that would permit terminally ill patients to refuse treatment in favor of death, but stops short of legalizing euthanasia; law is quiet coda to dramatic mercy killing of severely disabled man in 2003; it allows families to end life support for patients in coma, as in Terri Schiavo case, and permits doctors to prescribe pain medication for terminally ill patients even if those drugs may hasten death; it does not allow doctors to act to end patient's life, even at patient's request; law formalizes what has been practice in French hospitals but has rarely risen to level of public debate that such cases have caused in US (M)

news.abstract: Asif Ali Zardari, the husband of Benazir Bhutto, a former Pakistani prime minister, returned to the eastern Pakistan city of Lahore on Saturday and was immediately taken into custody by state security forces.    Mr. Zardari, 50, an opposition politician, had moved to Dubai to meet his wife and three children after being released on bail last November. Before that, he had spent eight years in a Pakistani prison awaiting trial on corruption and murder charges.
news.title: Pakistani Politician Taken Into Custody

news.abstract: There was never doubt that Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, the Vatican's hard-line defender of the faith, would have a strong hand in selecting the next pope. But in the days of prayer and politics before the conclave, which begins on Monday, he has emerged as perhaps the surprise central figure: the man who could become the 265th pope, choose him or be the one other cardinals knock from the running.     Any talk of who will become the next pope is guesswork, echoes from cardinals and their staffs sworn to silence about one of the world's most elite and secretive gatherings.
news.title: Cardinals Align as Time Nears to Select Pope

news.abstract: The cooks and elevator operators have been sworn to secrecy. A smokestack has been placed on the Sistine Chapel's roof. And on Saturday, the cardinals who will elect Pope John Paul II's successor held their last formal meeting.    Most details have been tied up ahead of Monday's conclave, the secret gathering of the princes of the church that will end when white smoke emerges to signal that they have chosen a new pope.
news.title: Cardinals Finish Preparations for Conclave

news.abstract: One day before a high-level Japanese visit aimed at defusing rising tensions between the countries, thousands of Chinese surrounded the Japanese Consulate here in an angry daylong demonstration.     After a three-hour march that began on the Shanghai riverfront, steadily gaining strength along a 10-mile route, well over 10,000 Chinese gathered at the consulate chanting anti-Japanese slogans and throwing a variety of missiles -- from heavy chunks of pavement to paint balloons and bottles -- at the consulate while several thousand law enforcement agents looked on passively.
news.title: China Allows More Protests in Shanghai Against Japan

news.abstract: Two more men were detained on suspicion of involvement in the attempted murder of Anatoly B. Chubais, chief of Russia's electricity monopoly and the architect of Russia's privatization in the 1990's. Mr. Chubais, one of Russia's most controversial men, was ambushed in his armored BMW outside Moscow last month and survived both a roadside bomb and gunfire. A former military intelligence colonel was already under arrest in the case, and the Interfax news agency reported that the new suspects had served with him. The authorities released few other details.   C.J. Chivers (NYT)

news.abstract: The third and final round of voting in Saudi Arabia's landmark, if partial, municipal elections unrolled in the western regions of the country, including the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. As in the previous rounds on Feb. 10 and March 3, only men over 21 were voting for a total 244 council seats in contention. Nationwide, the decision to elect nearly 600 members of the 178 councils, with the other half appointed, was seen as a first, limited step toward meeting demands for greater public participation in decision-making in the absolute monarchy. Candidates backed by prominent Muslim clergymen dominated the elections in major cities in the previous rounds.   Neil MacFarquhar (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Middle East: Saudi Arabia: Last Round Of Voting

news.abstract: Andrés Manuel López Obrador, above at center, the popular left-wing mayor of Mexico City and front-runner for president, may be the only politician in the world trying to have himself put in jail. Yesterday he went with supporters -- and a throng of reporters -- to the courthouse where the federal case against him on contempt-of-court charges is being heard and demanded that his bail be revoked so he could be imprisoned. A judge refused. On Wednesday, federal prosecutors presented the charges -- that he ignored a court order in 2001 -- but robbed him of the chance to look like a martyr for democracy by having two allies of President Vicente Fox pay his bail. Mr. López Obrador says the charges are trumped up and intended to knock him off the presidential ballot next year. He has vowed to run from jail if necessary. Meanwhile, he seems to be holding his own in polls. A poll by the newspaper El Universal indicated that his lead over candidates from the other two major parties had grown by three percentage points, to 38 percent over all, from 35 percent in February, which was before the government announced it would prosecute him and possibly push him out of the presidential race next year.   James C. McKinley Jr. (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Americas: Mexico: Still Trapped Outside Prison

news.abstract: With elections less than two months away, Iran's presidential hopefuls are scrambling to lure voters, promising everything from lowering the soaring prices of fruit and vegetables to normalizing relations with the country's longtime foe, the United States.    But much of the public is deeply apathetic. There is no real chance for a candidate who can spearhead the democratic changes once promised by the departing president, Mohammad Khatami, who proved unable to ward off the encroachment of the Guardian Council and its repressive agenda. Over the last eight years, the opposition has been marginalized as the judiciary has shut down more than 100 pro-change newspapers and journals and jailed dozens of advocates and intellectuals.
news.title: Promises ($60 for Instance) Fail to Rouse Iran's Voters

news.abstract: When Secretary General Kofi Annan declared in an unguarded moment last week that Saddam Hussein made most of his money ''on the American and British watch'' rather than from the United Nations oil-for-food program, he was expressing a view that is widely held but seldom uttered at the organization as it tries to avoid clashing with Washington.    Speaking to former United Nations communications officials and thinking his comments were confidential, Mr. Annan said Mr. Hussein pocketed far more from sanctions-skirting oil sales to Jordan and Turkey, which were being monitored by the United States and Britain, than from the scandal-tainted relief program run by the Security Council. ''They were the ones who had interdiction,'' he said. ''Possibly they were also the ones who knew exactly what was going on, and the countries themselves decided to close their eyes to smuggling to Turkey and Jordan because they were allies.''
news.title: Annan Remark on Oil Sales Draws Nods of Agreement

news.abstract: While officials say that the leak-prone Big Dig tunnel project is safe for motorists, they can give no assurance that taxpayers will not be soaked more to pay for repairs.    Kenneth Mead, the inspector general for the United States Department of Transportation, told a Congressional panel on Friday that years of scant independent financial oversight and the partnership forged by the Big Dig project manager and the state agency overseeing the plan could make assigning blame for problems with the tunnel difficult.
news.title: Big Dig Called Safe for Cars, but Not So for Pocketbooks

news.abstract: The leaders of Japan and China pledged to improve ties Saturday after weeks of escalating disputes, easing tension but not resolving some critical problems besieging relations between East Asia's big powers.    After a 55-minute meeting on the sidelines of an Asia-Africa summit conference here, Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi of Japan said both sides had agreed to look beyond disagreements and focus on the future.
news.title: China and Japan Leaders Pledge to Improve Relations

news.abstract: The issue of immigration moved to the center of Britain's election debate on Friday but here, among the grocers of Surrey Street market and the downtown shopping malls, many people seemed to have already drawn their conclusions.    This town on London's southern fringe is widely known as the headquarters of the British Home Office immigration authority, located in a bleak high-rise called Lunar House.
news.title: British Election Debates Spotlight Immigration Fears

news.abstract: Iraq's National Assembly votes overwhelmingly to approve Shiite-led cabinet, creating first fully and freely elected government in Iraqi history; divisions that delayed government's formation for three months after elections become apparent immediately; leader of Shiite political alliance that dominates assembly and cabinet delivers fiery speech hinting at purges to come in government's security forces; Sunni assembly member then accuses Shiites of dividing country; Sunni Arabs, who dominated Iraq's government under Saddam Hussein, largely boycotted Jan elections; now they say they are being 'marginalized' by 'government of winners'; cabinet remains incomplete; assembly's political factions have not yet agreed on candidates for five important ministries--defense, oil, electricity, industry and human rights; new government, when it assumes power early next week, will face extraordinary array of challenges, from guiding effort to write new constitution to rebuilding Iraq's shattered cities and fighting undiminished insurgency; photo; chart comparing positions held by minority groups and women in interim and transitional governments (M)

news.abstract: Eighteen new cases of polio have been found in Yemen, and the country is ''now facing a major epidemic,'' Dr. David L. Heymann, the chief of polio eradication for the World Health Organization, said in Geneva. Four cases were identified in the Red Sea port of Al Hudaida on April 20, but the new ones have been found across the country, including in the capital, Sana. Yemen had been polio-free since 1996. Dr. Bruce Aylward, who coordinates the W.H.O. eradication campaign, said testing ''quite clearly'' showed that the strain had arrived recently and had come from Kano, in Nigeria, by way of Chad and Port Sudan, across the Red Sea. Yemen, worried about outbreaks in Sudan and Saudi Arabia, held a vaccination day for children this month, and more are planned. Health authorities are using a new monovalent oral vaccine that needs fewer doses to create immunity to type 1 polio, the strain circulating in Yemen.   Donald G. McNeil Jr. (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Middle East: Yemen: 18 New Cases Of Polio Found

news.abstract: When Ainur Tairova realized she was on her way to her wedding, she started choking the driver.    Her marriage was intended to be to a man she had met only the day before, and briefly at that. Several of his friends had duped her into getting into a car; they picked up the would-be groom and then headed for his home.
news.title: Abduction, Often Violent, a Kyrgyz Wedding Rite

news.abstract: Insurgents determined to destabilize Iraq's new government executed a devastating series of coordinated attacks on Iraqi forces on Friday, detonating 12 car bombs across greater Baghdad and striking military targets throughout Iraq. At least 40 people were killed and more than 100 others wounded.    The attacks, a direct challenge to the new Shiite-dominated government that was formed Thursday, were aimed at Iraqi police officers and national guardsmen at their bases and traveling in convoys in northern and southern Baghdad and in Madaen, 15 miles southeast of the capital. At least 23 Iraqi policemen and troops were killed. Some reports put the total death toll at as many as 50 people.
news.title: Wave of Attacks in Iraq Kill 40 and Wound 100

news.abstract: Seven months before Sept. 11, 2001, the State Department issued a human rights report on Uzbekistan. It was a litany of horrors.    The police repeatedly tortured prisoners, State Department officials wrote, noting that the most common techniques were ''beating, often with blunt weapons, and asphyxiation with a gas mask.'' Separately, international human rights groups had reported that torture in Uzbek jails included boiling of body parts, using electroshock on genitals and plucking off fingernails and toenails with pliers. Two prisoners were boiled to death, the groups reported. The February 2001 State Department report stated bluntly, ''Uzbekistan is an authoritarian state with limited civil rights.''
news.title: U.S. Recruits a Rough Ally to Be a Jailer

news.abstract: In a country better known for copying and improving others' creations, the invention that was born here in rural Japan in 1993, at a 400-employee company surrounded by farmland, promised nothing less than a better light bulb.    In fact, it was the Holy Grail of lighting technology: the blue light-emitting diode, or L.E.D., which made white light a reality. It offers the prospect of a cheap, long-lasting light source that is expected to, someday soon, replace Edison's incandescent light bulb.
news.title: A Jolt to Team Japan: Bonus Demands

news.abstract: Egyptian authorities sweep through villages on outskirts of Cairo, detaining more than 200 people day after attacks that left seven people wounded and three attackers dead; police say most detainees are being investigated for connection to local terrorist networks; say one of dead attackers was suspect in deadly bombing Apr 7 at Cairo's main bazaar (M)
news.title: Egypt Detains More Than 200 in Attacks on Tourist Industry

news.abstract: Chairman of Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen Richard B Myers reportedly tells Congress in classified report that Pentagon's ability to deal with potential armed conflicts around world would be limited because of concentration of American troops and weapons in Iraq and Afghanistan; says any major combat operations elsewhere in world would probably be more protracted and produce higher American and foreign civilian casualties as result; says factors that would limit Pentagon's ability to prevail as quickly as war planners once predicted in other potential conflicts include reduced stockpiles of precision weapons, which were depleted during invasion of Iraq, and stress on reserve units, which fulfill bulk of combat support duties in Iraq; but despite limitations, Myers is unwavering in his assessment that American forces would win any major combat operation and are 'fully capable' of meeting all Washington's military objectives; just last week Pres Bush claimed that number of American troops in Iraq would not limit Washington's military options elsewhere; photo (M)
news.title: Pentagon Says Iraq Effort Limits Ability to Fight Other Conflicts
Philippines judged 'most murderous' place for journalists

news.abstract: The United States military released 85 Afghan prisoners from detention at its two main air bases in Bagram and Kandahar on Sunday and handed them over to Afghan authorities. They were mostly from south and southeastern Afghanistan and had been held for up to two years. They met with the country's chief justice, who urged them to participate in the peace process and reconstruction before he allowed them to go home.   Carlotta Gall (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Asia: Afghanistan: 85 Afghans Freed
More threats from N. Korea?
EU hopes to soften Japan fears over China
Victory Day holiday inflames old wounds
Goodbye Uncle Sam?

news.abstract: House and Senate conference agrees to final version of $82 billion supplementary spending bill for wars in Iraq and Afghanistan; measure includes $75.9 billion for military operations as well as other money to increase death benefits to military families, to bolster United States border security, and to provide aid to Palestinians (S)
news.title: House and Senate Reach Accord on $82 Billion for Costs of Wars
Army rigged Guantánamo interrogations, author says
French investigate Chinese woman's files
Iraq war could steal votes for Blair

news.abstract: Prosecutors in Vancouver said they will not appeal the acquittal of two Sikh men who were charged in the 1985 bombing of Air India Flight 182, which exploded and crashed off Ireland while flying from Toronto to India, killing 329. In a ruling in March, the judge in the case said the prosecution's chief witnesses against the two men, Ripudaman Singh Malik, 58, and Ajaib Singh Bagri, 55, were not credible. Prosecutors have now concluded that there were no legal errors in the ruling that would allow an appeal. The decision was met with disappointment from the victim's families, who continue to demand a federal inquiry into the failure of the 20-year case.   Colin Campbell (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Americas: Canada: No Appeal Of Verdict In Air India Bombing

news.abstract: Republican chairman of Senate Foreign Relations Committee declines to endorse Democratic request that State Dept turn over documents related to long-running dispute between John R Bolton and American intelligence agencies over assessments about Syria and its weapons program; move is blow to Democrats on panel, who have focused on dispute as central part of their effort to defeat Bolton's nomination as ambassador to United Nations (M)
news.title: A Setback to Democrats' Request for Papers on Bolton and Syria
Heavy fighting in the southeastern Afghanistan

news.abstract: Labor Party is expected to be overall winner in British elections, but lackluster win would have far-reaching political consequences for Prime Min Tony Blair; key to outcome is likely to be in places where Labor Party has only slender lead on Conservatives and where older people are far more likely to determine outcome of vote than young; photo (M)
news.title: As Britain Votes, Tight Races for Older Voters Hold the Key
2 explosions near British Consulate

news.abstract: At least 22 people are killed when Iraqi insurgents stage series of attacks across Baghdad, including suicide attack amid crowd of job applicants outside Iraqi Army base; insurgents have seized on indecision of new Shiite-led government and Sunni Arabs over unfilled cabinet posts to mount increasinlgy deadly attacks; in Mosul, car bomb kills four policemen; photo (M)
news.title: Insurgents Press Attacks on Iraq Security Forces, Killing 22
Acquittal denied, defense in Jackson case takes stage
Malays reject accusations they aid Thai separatists

news.abstract: Britain's political landscape was redrawn on Friday after a tumultuous election that gave Prime Minister Tony Blair a third term with a severely reduced majority, strengthening rivals within and outside his Labor Party, and hastened the departure of Michael Howard as the leader of the opposition Conservatives.    Mr. Howard announced that he would step down ''sooner rather than later'' after he increased his party's representation in the 646-seat Parliament but failed to ignite broader appeal beyond the bedrock Conservative base.
news.title: A Wounded Blair, Rivals Strengthened, Begins Third Term; Tory Leader to Step Down

news.abstract: Leonid Shamkovich, Russian-born chess grandmaster, dies at age 81 (M)
news.title: Leonid Shamkovich, 81, Ex-Soviet Chess Grandmaster, Is Dead
Briefly: EU reports evidence of fraud in Togo vote

news.abstract: The Department of Defense has identified 1,589 American service members who have died since the start of the Iraq war. It confirmed the death of the following American yesterday:      BROOKS, William J., 30, Staff Sgt., Army; Birmingham, Ala.; Third Armored Division.
news.title: Names of the Dead
Hamas makes strong election showing

news.abstract: For more than two years, critics who accused the Bush administration of improperly using political influence to shape intelligence assessments have, for the most part, failed to make the charge stick. On Iraq, the main focus of scrutiny, two official inquiries have blamed intelligence agencies for inflating the threat posed by Baghdad's illicit weapons, but have stopped short of blaming political pressures for the problem.    Those findings have never fully satisfied many intelligence officials and some administration critics. At minimum, they have said, some senior Bush administration officials have played an unhelpful role, by urging intelligence agencies to revise conclusions in a direction more consistent with administration policy, as in pursuing links between Iraq and Al Qaeda.
news.title: Tug of War: Intelligence vs. Politics

news.abstract: The leaders met in what was widely expected to be a tense encounter, but advisers to both men moved swiftly to pronounce the meeting a success.
news.title: Amid Tensions, Bush and Putin Conduct Meeting in Russia
Eleven killed, 162 wounded in rebel bombings in Myanmar capital

news.abstract: WASHINGTON, May 8 - The chairman of the Senate intelligence committee said today that he believed North Korea appeared to be preparing a nuclear test explosion, even as the head of the United Nations nuclear monitoring agency said he believed the North had five or six nuclear weapons in its possession.
news.title: Chair of Senate Intelligence Committee Believes North Korea Is Preparing Nuclear Test

news.abstract: Voters in Northern Ireland have delivered convincing victories to hard-line parties in Britain's parliamentary elections, stoking fears that a resumption of the suspended Northern Irish legislature, which is intended to provide power-sharing between Roman Catholic and Protestant groups, will be more difficult.     The results moved Northern Ireland closer to a two-party system after decades in which voters could choose from a spectrum of moderate opinion.
news.title: Hard-Liners in Northern Ireland Gain in British Voting, Leaving Peace Pact in Jeopardy

news.abstract: The British prime minister gave his first foreign interview to the German newspaper Bild Zeitung, a racy daily known for reducing foreign policy issues to basics.
news.title: Blair Brushes Aside Stereotypes to Praise British-German Relations

news.abstract: Bush administration officials say they have no idea where Pres Bush's place will be, who he will stand near, at Pres Vladimir V Putin's celebration of 60th anniversary of German defeat in World War II; there is speculation about what he would say if he stands near any foreign leader he has called a dictator (White House Letter) (M)
news.title: Guest List at Putin's Party Could Become an Event
Vatican ousts U.S. editor

news.abstract: China is being pressured to abolish or change its vast system of re-education camps that operate outside court system; estimated 300,000 prostitutes, drug users, petty criminals, members of Falun Gong and other political prisoners have been stripped of any legal rights and locked inside vast penal system that is separate from judicial system; system, relic of Mao era, is major tool Communist Party uses to maintain hold on power and social order; it allows police to sweep up masses of people without time and complications of court trials; China is facing pressure at home and abroad to change; key members of European Union express reluctance to lift arms embargo without significant gesture by China on human rights; outside China, Falun Gong is waging aggressive campaign to pubilcize its allegations of mistreatment, which Chinese government denies; history of labor re-education camps detailed; photo; map (M)
news.title: Issue in China: Many in Jails Without Trial

news.abstract: State Dept refuses to make public internal documents sought by Senate Democrats in their attempt to seek more information about repeated clashes between John R Bolton and American intelligence agencies over Syria; Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice says information involves 'internal deliberations' and their disclosure could have chilling effect on debates within administration; Bolton has been chosen by Pres Bush to be ambassador to United Nations (M)
news.title: Rice's Reason for Withholding Bolton Files: A Chilling Effect

news.abstract: Marine task force sweeps through wide area of westen Iraq near Syrian border, killing 100 insurgents and raiding desert outposts and city safe houses they use to import cars, money, weapons and foreigners to fight United States and Iraqi forces; senior American commanders blame porous border with Syria for allowing never-ending stream of armed jihadists to enter Iraq and replenish insurgency as quickly as fighters are killed or captured; say new offensive, largest since Marines invaded Falluja six months ago, was spurred by new intelligence gleaned from Iraqis living in area as well as interrogations of newly captured aides to Abu Musab al-Zarqawi, most wanted terrorist in Iraq; Iraq's new defense minister Sadoon al-Dulaimi says he will continue military policies set by departing administration of Ayad Allawi, who aggressively pursued operations against insurgents; photo; map (M)
news.title: 100 Rebels Killed in U.S. Offensive in Western Iraq

news.abstract: Insurgents who control parts of the western Iraqi desert appeared to have fallen back as the Marines prepared a new assault.
news.title: U.S. Says Fighting Pauses in Western Iraq as Rebels Regroup

news.abstract: Mayor Andrés Manuel López Obrador of Mexico City said he would step down on July 31 to begin campaigning for his party's presidential nomination. Mr. López Obrador, of the leftist Democratic Revolutionary Party, leads all national polls ahead of next year's election. His popularity soared even as the federal government sought to prosecute him over a minor land dispute. It dropped the charges last week.   Antonio Betancourt (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Americas: Mexico: Mayor To Quit To Seek Presidency
U.S. needs a 'break' in troop withdrawals

news.abstract: After six months of exceptionally dry weather, the government has begun restricting water use in preparation for the first major drought in 10 years, an official at the Environmental Ministry said. Average precipitation across Spain this winter measured less than 3 inches, or 35 percent of typical levels. Forecasts show few signs that rainfall will increase significantly over the summer. The restrictions apply so far just to water used for irrigating crops. Officials in the agricultural industry, particularly in the olive and cereal sectors, have warned that their crops could be seriously damaged by the restrictions.   Renwick McLean (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Europe: Spain: Measures To Combat Drought

news.abstract: Less than two weeks after suspending emergency rule, King Gyanendra got a nod of support from two of his most important allies. India announced that it would resume military aid, suspended since the king dismissed the government on Feb. 1 and took direct power, and the United States said it backed him against the country's Maoist insurgency. The American support came on a visit by the assistant secretary of state for South Asia, Christina Rocca, above. She is the highest ranking American official to visit since the royal takeover, and she urged the palace to free political prisoners, reinstate civil liberties and reach out to political parties. The United States also cut military aid, and she did not say when it might be restored.   Somini Sengupta (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Asia: Nepal: U.S. Backs Fight Against Rebels

news.abstract: Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi of Japan downplayed Pyongyang's statement, calling it "gamesmanship."
news.title: North Korea Says It Has Pulled Nuclear Rods From Reactor

news.abstract: Germany's much debated and long-awaited Holocaust memorial opens, Berlin; Parliament president Wolfgang Thierse speaks, rite attended Chanceller Gerhard Schroder and all senior government officials; Peter Eisenman designed memorial; photo (M)
news.title: Holocaust Memorial Opens in Berlin

news.abstract: A fire that gutted a historic synagogue in Malakhovka, just outside Moscow, may have been arson, a police official told the Itar-Tass news agency. A village official and Russia's chief rabbi, Berl Lazar, said they also believed it to be arson. The synagogue, which had also been burglarized over the weekend, was built to look like a shed in the 1930's, when religion was brutally persecuted in the Soviet Union.   Sophia Kishkovsky (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Europe: Russia: Arson Suspected In Synagogue Fire
Insurgents kill 60 in spate of attacks across country

news.abstract: The environment minister, Dick Roche, issued licenses for the excavation of archaeological sites around the Hill of Tara, effectively approving construction of a highway that will run adjacent to Tara, the 4,000-year-old site that is the burial place of 140 kings. Hundreds of historians and archaeologists, and the government's cultural advisers, have campaigned against the roadway's path, and its planners would have been forced to explore an alternative route if Mr. Roche had withheld the licenses.   Brian Lavery (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Europe: Ireland: Approval For Highway Near Ancient Site

news.abstract: Reporter's Notebook on Pres Bush's encounter with stick shift on Russian Pres Vladimir Putin's gleamingly restored 1956 Volga, parked outside Putin's dacha; American reporters with Bush in Moscow are barred from military parade marking 60th anniversary of defeat of Nazis, but amuse themselves by watching glitzy production on Russian television; cameras catch Bush with other leaders, although not any out-of-favor dictators or former dictators; Bush, traveling on to Georgia, commiserates with Pres Mikhail Saakashvili about press (M)
news.title: Putin Helps Bush Get Into Gear for Friendly Photo Opportunity
North Korea unloads atom fuel

news.abstract: Names of four Americans newly confirmed dead in Iraq; 1,601 American service members have died since start of war
news.title: Names of the Dead

news.abstract: Four protesters are killed and more than 60 injured in Jalalabad as Afghan police and troops struggle to contain anti-American demonstrations; photo; map; religious hard-liners and armed man apparently usurp what started as student protest (M)
news.title: Afghan Protest Against the U.S. Becomes Violent
German lower house approves EU charter

news.abstract: Military proseuctors in trial of Specialist Sabrina Harman, former Abu Ghraib prison guard, say photographs, including one of hooded detainee standing on box with wires in his hand, are irrefutable evidence of guard's guilt; case against Harman is largely based on photos she took or posed in; her defense team notes that Harman was lowest-ranking soldier among those prosecuted in scandal, and that she was repulsed by abuses which she reported to superiors, to no avail; photo (M)
news.title: Court-Martial Opens in an Iraqi Abuse Case

news.abstract: European Human Rights Court upholds earlier decision that 1999 trial of Kurdish separatist leader Abdullah Ocalan was unfair and that Turkey should reopen case; cites extended period of time he was held before standing trial and limited time given for him to prepare defense; Turkey could jeopardize its application to join European Union if it refuses to revisit case; many people in Turkey worry that reopening case could reignite fires of Kurdish nationalism; it could also rekindle sense of Turkish nationalism, which could further complicate country's efforts to join EU; although court is not European Union body, defying its wishes could put Turkey in breach of European Convention on Human Rights, to which all EU members must belong (M)
news.title: European Court Urges Turkey to Grant Kurdish Leader a New Trial

news.abstract: Italy's highest court ruled that a man who married without telling his bride that he was impotent denied her the ''right to sexuality'' and possibly motherhood and ordered him to pay her damages, Italian news media reported. The amount of damages will be decided by another court. The couple married in the 1990's without having had sex, and the woman learned of her new husband's condition on their wedding night. The marriage was later annulled, but the woman demanded damages for his lack of ''fairness and good faith'' before their wedding and for his refusal to seek treatment afterward because his condition would then become known to someone else.   Jason Horowitz (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Europe: Italy: Conjugal Duty Is A Legal Duty, Court Rules
Car bomb kills 12 in Baghdad
Measured hopes for a fledging East Timor
Belgian leader survives linguistic crisis

news.abstract: In the name of fraternity, the French are feuding.    The bickering is over Pentecost, the Christian feast commemorating the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles on the 50th day after the Resurrection of Christ. The day after, Pentecost Monday, has long been celebrated in France as a paid holiday.
news.title: 'Day of Solidarity' Shouldn't Include Work, French Say

news.abstract: One morning last month, Qasim al-Malakh, one of Iraq's best-known actors, stood near a dusty vacant lot in a dangerous part of southern Baghdad. He was dressed immaculately in a dark suit and tie, and his co-star, Nagham al-Sultani, stood next to him in a white bridal gown.    They were there to film the last episode of ''Love and War,'' Iraq's most popular television drama. Their characters, Fawzi and Fatin, had just married after a long and troubled romance.
news.title: Tragicomedy of Life in Baghdad Is Brought Home in a TV Series

news.abstract: Two and a half years after a mysterious respiratory illness from southern China infected thousands of people around the world and brought dire predictions of recurring and deadly plague, the virus known as SARS has again provided a surprise.    It has disappeared, at least for the moment.
news.title: After Its Epidemic Arrival, SARS Vanishes

news.abstract: The Department of Defense has identified 1,612 American service members who have died since the start of the Iraq war. It confirmed the deaths of the following Americans on Friday:    JODON, Andrew R., 27, Sgt., Army; Karthaus, Pa.; Third Infantry Division.    ZEIGLER, Kenneth E. II, 22, Pfc., Army; Dillsburg, Pa.; Third Infantry Division.
news.title: Names of the Dead

news.abstract: It happens discreetly, unnoticed by other passengers. The traveler, usually a middle-aged man, gets off the plane at a Dutch airport where plainclothes officials politely receive him. He is escorted to a vehicle and, before long, he disappears behind the walls of a high-security jail near The Hague.    Thus, another war crimes suspect is checked in at the compound where the United Nations has its own cellblock.
news.title: Court on Crimes in Former Yugoslavia Hits Its Stride

news.abstract: The United States has warned four nations campaigning jointly for permanent seats on the United Nations Security Council that it will not support their cause unless they agree not to ask for the veto power that the five current permanent Council members hold, senior diplomats and administration officials said.     The four nations -- Brazil, India, Germany and Japan -- are unhappy about that position. ''The Security Council is not like an aircraft, with first class, business and economy seats,'' said Ryozo Kato, Japan's ambassador to the United States.
news.title: As Nations Lobby to Join Security Council, the U.S. Resists Giving Them Veto Power

news.abstract: President Hamid Karzai returned from a trip to drum up more aid from Europe on Saturday to express shame and frustration at the violence that has racked Afghanistan over the last five days, leaving at least 17 dead and many wounded.    At his heavily guarded office in Kabul, he blamed ''enemies of peace'' and ''enemies of stability'' for violently subverting students' protests over recent reports that American interrogators at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, had desecrated a Koran.
news.title: Karzai Says Afghan Progress Is Protests' Real Target
Adventurer finds challenge in a city of extremes
Seattle leads U.S. cities joining Kyoto Protocol
U.S. warns N. Korea on atomic test

news.abstract: The judges began reading their verdict against Mikhail B. Khodorkovsky, but then postponed the final verdict for at least another day.
news.title: Russian Court Suspends Reading of Verdict Against Billionaire

news.abstract: Bush administration warns North Korea that if it conducts nuclear test, United States and several Pacific powers would take punitive action, but does not specify what kind of sanctions would result; Pres Bush's national security adviser Stephen J Hadley calls North Korea 'hard target' whose intentions are nearly impossible to assess, but his warnings represent first time anyone in Bush administration has drawn 'red line' that North Korea could not cross without prompting reaction; Bush's aides have said over past year that drawing clear line would be seen by North Koreans as challenge; they say concerns about baiting North Korea could explain why Hadley did not specify what kind of penalty is possible; Shinzo Abe, secretary general of Japan's governing party, says that if North Korea conducts nuclear tests, Japan would go to Security Council before imposing sanctions; photo (M)
news.title: U.S. Is Warning North Koreans on Nuclear Test
Two Koreas resume talks after 10-month hiatus

news.abstract: Government of Uzbekistan maintains that it acted cautiously and minimized use of force in putting down prison break and demonstration, but survivors with gunshot wounds dispute this; they say security forces fired indiscriminately at unarmed civilians, striking women and children in public square in Andijon with little warning; say many civilians had gathered in square in hope of seeing Pres Islam A Karimov, to complain about joblessness and poverty; say they were met by troops instead; Karimov blames unrest on Islamic extremist groups; photo (M) with
news.title: Uzbeks Say Troops Shot Recklessly at Civilians

news.abstract: France is thrown into confusion by well-meaning government initiative to sacrifice paid holiday to raise money for country's elderly; main unions urge their workers to strike, and almost half the country stays home; many town halls throughout country are closed, and dozens of cities and towns are without most public transportation; schools operate according to whimsy of their principals and teachers; government challenges assumption that initiative has failed; photo (M)
news.title: French Lose a Holiday, but Many, Angry, Take One Anyway
Italian CARE worker kidnapped in Kabul

news.abstract: Afghan security officials report kidnapping of Clementina Cantoni, Italian woman working for CARE International; say she was abducted in Kabul, second kidnapping of foreigner in six months in country; it comes after several days of worst anti-Western violence there since American intervention in wake of 9/11; just last week CARE issued report about deteriorating security in Afghanistan, which it said was hampering work of aid organizations there; photos (M)
news.title: Gunmen in Afghan Capital Kidnap Italian CARE Worker

news.abstract: George Galloway, maverick member of British Parliament, denies to US Senate Permanent Committee on Investigations as 'absolutely preposterous' committee's charges that Saddam Hussein's government had given him rights to buy 20 million barrels of oil to sell at profit; his appearance seems to catch Senate committee off guard; Galloway also uses committee's invitation to testify under oath to turn tables on his accusers, charging that commitee had 'found me guilty' without having given him opportunity to defend himself against allegations that he had profited from United Nations oil-for-food program; photo (M)
news.title: British Lawmaker Scolds Senators on Iraq
Spain gives EU treaty final backing

news.abstract: British authorities are mystified as to identity of man who was found wandering on beach in damp clothes on Isle of Sheppey in Kent; he was wearing dark suit and white shirt; labels had been cut out from his clothes so they offered no clues to his identity; he may be man suffering from amnesia after terrible shock of some kind; nothing can be confirmed as he has not spoken or communicated in words--spoken or written--since he was found; all that is known is that when people who cared for him gave him pencil and paper in early April, he drew grand piano casting deep shadow; and when they took him to piano in hospital chapel he was transformed, playing fluently in what seemed classical style; photo (M)
news.title: A Silent Man Who Excels at the Piano Baffles Britain

news.abstract: Bolivian Pres Carlos Mesa's government allows passage of bill that will sharply raise taxes on foreign energy companies, move officials hope will defuse mounting protests from groups that want Bolivia to squeeze big multinationals that have flocked to this poor country; but decision by Mesa, who has bowed repeatedly to demands from protesters in his 19-month term, appears to placate few; foreign oil companies say law is financially onerous and will prompt them to cut back on investments; thousands of Indians and miners continue to march from several communities in highlands toward capital, some of their leaders promising to take over Congress unless tougher law is approved; photo (M)
news.title: Foreign Gas Companies in Bolivia Face Sharply Higher Taxes
North Koreans resist appeal to rejoin talks

news.abstract: Israel carries out its first airstrike since truce was announced three months ago, firing on Palestinian cell that was firing mortars at Jewish settlements in southern Gaza Strip; one Palestinian militant is dead and several are wounded, as is one Israeli civilian; events reflect fragile nature of truce that has greatly reduced overall level of violence since Feb but has not silenced the guns (M)
news.title: Israel Carries Out First Airstrike, in Gaza, in 3 Months of Truce
Leave rules to us, sports chiefs say

news.abstract: Leading Sunni cleric in Iraq Sheik Harith al-Dari publicly accuses Shiite militia of killing Sunni clerics; charge seen as troubling sign of rising tensions between Iraq's two main religious groups; Dari charges that militia group known as Badr Brigade killed Sunni clerics, including one whose body was found May 15 in Shiite area of Baghdad; commander of Badr Brigade denies charge and blames hard-line Sunni Islamists and former members of Saddam Hussein's government for killings (M)
news.title: Sunni Accuses a Shiite Militia of Killing Clerics

news.abstract: Rev Jesse L Jackson, in visit to Mexico, says Pres Vicente Fox's recent derogatory remark about African-Americans was 'offensive' but may force Mexico to give blacks place in its negotiations with United States on variety of issues; some commentators in Mexico say Fox inadvertently exposed disturbing reality, that his comments were not uncommon among Mexicans who typically pride themselves on being colorblind society; photo (M)
news.title: Uneasily, a Latin Land Looks at Its Own Complexion

news.abstract: North Korea did not promise to return to six-nation talks aimed at ending the Communist state's nuclear weapons program.
news.title: Koreas End Talks, Resuming High-Level Ties

news.abstract: A file of an inquiry into the deaths of two detainees at Bagram, Afghanistan, depicts repeated harsh treatment of prisoners.
news.title: In U.S. Report, Brutal Details of 2 Afghan Inmates' Deaths
Japan cool to China bid for a free trade accord
Election over, Zimbabwe is back to bad old days
Israeli defense chief issues warning on rockets

news.abstract: Shiite-led Iraqi government publicly acknowledges for first time that Iraq was aggressor in 1980 when it touched off bloody eight-year war with Iran; statement comes at end of three-day visit by Iranian Foreign Min Kamal Kharazi; it is likely to inflame further resentment of Iraq's Sunni Arabs, who ran country at time of that war; Iran has long sought formal recognition of Iraq's use of chemical weapons against it during war (M)
news.title: Iraqi Government, in Statement With Iran, Admits Fault for 1980's War
Army file details deaths of Afghan detainees

news.abstract: A 16-year-old girl was arrested and charged with being part of a group of youths that attacked another girl in Manchester while filming the incident on a mobile telephone. The victim, 16-year-old Becky Smith, was briefly knocked out and spent two days in the hospital with head injuries. The assault was the latest example of an apparent British craze known as ''happy slapping,'' in which youths randomly attack passers-by and then use their mobile phones to circulate pictures of the victims. Miss Smith's mother, Georgina, said that video phones should be banned from schools.   Sarah Lyall (NYT)
news.title: World Briefing | Europe: Britain: Girl, 16, Held In 'Happy Slap' Attack
Some settlers in Gaza still plan to stay put

news.abstract: A front-page photograph of Saddam Hussein in his underwear in an Iraqi prison greeted readers of The New York Post and The Sun in London yesterday, coming to The Sun from an American military source seeking to weaken the Iraqi insurgency, The Post reported.     The photo of Mr. Hussein in briefs and the story of how the tabloid newspapers obtained the images quickly became television news, and print journalists as well struggled with how they would handle the provocative report.
news.title: Prison Images Raise Issues for World Media
China opening door to Taiwan

news.abstract: The founder of a Roman Catholic order in Mexico will not face a church trial on allegations that he molested teenagers, a Vatican spokesman said.
news.title: Vatican Says Mexican Priest Will Not Face Abuse Trial

news.abstract: Despite autopsy findings of homicide and statements by soldiers that two prisoners died after being struck by guards at an American military detention center in Bagram, Afghanistan, Army investigators initially recommended closing the case without bringing any criminal charges, documents and interviews show.    Within days after the two deaths in December 2002, military coroners determined that both had been caused by ''blunt force trauma'' to the legs. Soon after, soldiers and others at Bagram told the investigators that military guards had repeatedly struck both men in the thighs while they were shackled and that one had also been mistreated by military interrogators.
news.title: Army Faltered in Investigating Detainee Abuse

news.abstract: ''The Child,'' a Belgian film directed by Jean-Pierre Dardenne and Luc Dardenne, won the Palme d'Or as best film at the 58th Cannes Film Festival on Saturday night.    The film, which follows a young petty thief as he struggles with the moral dilemmas of fatherhood, was inspired by Dostoyevsky's ''Crime and Punishment'' and influenced by the classic French film ''Pickpocket,'' by Robert Bresson.
news.title: Two Belgians Win Top Prize at Cannes for Second Time
North Korean ship makes historic trip to South

news.abstract: For a quarter of a century, it has been pretty much assumed in the half-dozen founding countries of the now 25-member European Union that popular support for an ever bigger and more unified Europe would be virtually automatic.     Not anymore. At least not if large segments of public opinion in the founding states of France and the Netherlands matter.
news.title: Charter for the European Union Meets Resistance
Monogolian voterschoose a president
A new breed of evangelicals joins U.S. elite
U.S. wants to know how Saddam photos got out
Briefly: 20 hurt as bombs target controversial movie

news.abstract: Gen Juan Emilio Cheyre, commander of Chilean Army, is being blamed by many for loss of at least 21 young, inexperienced recruits in Andean blizzard; since becoming commander three years ago, he has been one of Pres Ricardo Lagos's chief allies in working to overcome legacy of Pinochet years, apologizing for human rights abuses and repeatedly bowing to principle of civilian supremacy over armed forces at other critical moments; now grieving and irate parents wonder why their teenage sons were sent off ill prepared and ill equipped on their fatal mission; two colonels who led regiment involved in exercise have been stripped of their posts pending outcome of investigation; photo; map (M)
news.title: Andes Deaths Are Another Black Eye for Chile's Military

news.abstract: Iraqi officials cannot explain what happened to $69 million worth of fuel oil produced in the second half of 2004, raising fears that it was smuggled out of the country for private gain, according to a report released yesterday by United Nations-appointed auditors.     The report, by the auditing firm KPMG, said Iraq's recorded exports of fuel oil mysteriously declined by a comparable amount during that same period of 2004, the initial months of sovereignty for the newly installed Iraqi government.
news.title: Iraq Can't Explain $69 Million in Fuel Oil From '04, Audit Says

news.abstract: With grocery stores bereft of basic goods and the currency once more in free fall, Zimbabwe's government said Monday that it had rounded up more than 9,600 residents of the capital, Harare, in a crackdown on black-market peddlers and ''general lawlessness.''    The official explanation for the dragnet, announced in state-run newspapers, was that the raids were aimed at black-market profiteers who were hoarding commodities like cooking oil and corn meal, creating artificial shortages.
news.title: Dragnet Arrests in Zimbabwe Send Warning
Mongolia elects ex-prime minister

news.abstract: Over sausage sandwiches and vast amounts of beer and local wine, thousands of Frenchmen stood around and argued over how best to save France. Save France from Europe, that is: the Europe that France played a crucial role in building a half-century ago.    But now, say the anti-globalizers and anti-imperialists, the farmers and factory workers who crammed into the smoky exhibition hall in this southern city Friday, Europe has lost its way. They may be treated as traitors and imbeciles by their opponents, they add, but they call themselves patriots.
news.title: In Southern France, Strong Opposition to Europe Treaty

news.abstract: Insurgents carried out three major car bomb attacks against Iraqi Shiites on Monday, killing at least 33 and wounding 120 in what appeared to be the latest in a wave of violence intended to exploit the sectarian divisions that have tormented the country.    All told, attacks across Iraq killed at least 43 people, including Waiel al-Rubaie, a senior aide in Prime Minister Ibrahim al-Jaafari's administration, and his driver, who were shot to death in the Mansour district of Baghdad. The American military said three American soldiers were also killed in the northern city of Mosul on Sunday.
news.title: Car Bombings in Iraq Kill 33, With Shiites as Targets

news.abstract: Voters overwhelmingly approved a constitutional change to allow Egypt's first contested presidential election, Interior Minister Habib el-Adly announced on state-run television. He said that 83 percent of the voters in the referendum on Wednesday had backed the change and that 54 percent of the country's 32 million registered voters had participated. Opposition figures -- who had called for a boycott of the referendum -- quickly dismissed the figures. In Washington, President Bush criticized the government of President Hosni Mubarak for the violence during the voting, including the beating of opposition demonstrators. ''The idea of people expressing themselves in opposition to the government, then getting beaten, is not our view of how a democracy ought to work,'' Mr. Bush said. ''It's not the way that you have free elections.''   Hassan M. Fattah (NYT)

news.abstract: A posting on Friday on the Internet site for Al Qaeda in Mesopotamia, the group led by the Islamic militant Abu Musab al-Zarqawi, reversed two days of dire warnings about his condition and stated that he was ''in good health and runs the jihad operation by himself,'' according to the SITE Institute, a group that tracks the postings.    It was one in a series of conflicting statements in recent days about Mr. Zarqawi's health. On Tuesday, his group said he had been seriously injured and urged Muslims to pray for his recovery. On Thursday, postings on two different Islamist sites said after suffering a bullet wound in his lung, he had appointed a deputy to stand in for him and left Iraq to seek medical care.
news.title: Internet Site Says Zarqawi Is Healthy and in Charge

news.abstract: Sweden is days away from banning smoking in restaurants and bars, but the national passion for snuff will likely mean that the measure will be met with little protest.

news.abstract: From nuclear negotiators to student dissidents, from bazaar merchants to turbaned mullahs, Iranians agree: the right to develop nuclear power is a point of national pride.     ''For a country to have nuclear energy means that it has made progress in all other fields as well, so other countries have to respect its technology,'' said Nilufar, 29, a graduate student in energy management at the prestigious Sharif Industrial University. Nilufar, covered in black so only her face was showing, agreed to be interviewed on such a delicate topic only if her family name was not used.
news.title: Across Iran, Nuclear Power Is a Matter of Pride
Forensic officers search for clues amid debris of Indonesian bombs

news.abstract: The surge of violence that has swept Iraq since its first elected government took office nearly a month ago continued Saturday, with at least 30 new deaths reported across the country, some of them in what appeared to be sectarian killings.    The latest attacks raised the total number of Iraqis killed this month to about 650, in addition to at least 63 American troops who have been killed, the highest American toll since January.
news.title: Violence Surges Across Iraq With 30 New Deaths Reported

news.abstract: Nothing but the faint sound of birds nesting on surrounding hilltops can be heard inside this new mountaintop site -- part museum, part monument -- that is the first public commemoration of one of the darkest chapters in China's recent past.    Inside the circular pavilion that is the site's centerpiece, the walls are lined with a series of gray tablets, each starkly engraved with images depicting the Cultural Revolution, China's decade-long descent into madness, beginning in the mid-1960's.
news.title: Scenes From a Nightmare: A Shrine to the Maoist Chaos

news.abstract: Voters here kicked off the first of four rounds of voting for Parliament on Sunday in the first elections free of Syrian interference in more than three decades. A powerful slate led by the son of the assassinated former prime minister is heavily favored to sweep the vote.     Mohammad Taqoush, 25, went to the polls in the Ras Beirut neighborhood of West Beirut with high expectations. He marched in the demonstrations against the Syrian presence in Lebanon after the assassination of the former prime minister, Rafik Hariri, in February, and saw the vote as a moment for the former opposition to make good on its promises for change.
news.title: Turnout Is Low as Lebanon Begins Voting for Parliament

Nurgaliyev, told a meeting of ministry officials. About 700,000 children are orphans, he said, while two million adolescents are illiterate and four million use drugs. news.abstract: Oslo has offered a reward of $329,000 for information leading to the recovery of two Edvard Munch paintings, ''The Scream'' and ''Madonna,'' which were taken in a brazen daylight robbery of the Munch Museum last August. Four men have been jailed in the case, but formal charges have yet to be filed, a police spokesman said. ''We're optimistic the paintings will eventually turn up and hope the reward will shorten the time,'' said the spokesman, Morten Hojem Ervik.   Walter Gibbs (NYT)

news.abstract: Hoping to end mounting nationwide protests, President Carlos Mesa of Bolivia announced plans late Thursday for the election of a citizen assembly to write a new constitution and for a national referendum on greater regional autonomy.    With Congress deadlocked over the two popular demands, and with swarms of protesters paralyzing the country, Mr. Mesa told Bolivians in a nationally televised address that the election and referendum would take place Oct. 16. Political analysts say Congress must ratify the plan, but Mr. Mesa said he had to act fast.
news.title: Bolivian Offers Reform Plan to Protesters Seeking Autonomy

news.abstract: For weeks, sightings of Taliban fighters were being reported all over the rugged mountains here. But when Staff Sgt. Patrick Brannan and his team of scouts drove into a nearby village to investigate a complaint of a beating, they had no idea that they were stumbling into the biggest battle of their lives.    On May 3, joined by 10 local policemen and an interpreter, the scouts turned up at a kind of Taliban convention -- of some 60 to 80 fighters -- and were greeted by rockets and gunfire. The sergeant called for reinforcements and was told to keep the Taliban engaged until they arrived. ''I've only got six men,'' he remembers saying.
news.title: Despite Years of U.S. Pressure, Taliban Fight On in Jagged Hills
